title: Origen's therapeia toward Gabriel and Michael is acknowledgment and imitation, not invocation
source_text: LXX. Proinde quum Origenes octavo illo adversus Celsum libro, insinuat quandam θεραπείαν, id est, honoris & observantiae speciem veris Dei Ministris, Gabrieli, Michaeli, caeterisque Angelis & Archangelis deberi, θεραπεία ista, juxta doctrinam Origenis, nullo modo constitui potest in quadam eorum adoratione, & invocatione, quae in solidum & indivisibiliter uni summo Deo deberi contendit: sed in illa beatitudinis, gloriae & sanctitatis agnitione & celebratione, & etiam obsequii & amoris erga Deum pia imitatione, quibus Sanctos Angelos colere nos posse fatetur.
pass_a_gloss: Therefore when Origen in that eighth book against Celsus insinuates that a certain therapeia, that is, a kind of honor and observance, is owed to the true Ministers of God, Gabriel, Michael, and the other Angels and Archangels, that therapeia, according to the doctrine of Origen, can in no way be placed in some adoration of them, and invocation, which he contends is owed wholly and indivisibly to the one supreme God: but in that acknowledgment and celebration of blessedness, glory and holiness, and also the pious imitation of obedience and love toward God, by which he confesses that we can honor the Holy Angels.
pass_b_english: So when Origen, in that eighth book against Celsus, suggests that a certain therapeia, that is, a kind of honor and respect, is owed to God's true servants, Gabriel, Michael, and the other angels and archangels, that therapeia, by Origen's own teaching, can in no way consist in adoring or invoking them, which he insists is owed entirely and undivided to the one supreme God. It consists in acknowledging and celebrating their blessedness, glory, and holiness, and in devoutly imitating their obedience and love toward God. These are the ways in which he admits we may honor the holy angels.

choices.why: Le Blanc glosses the Greek himself; transliterating keeps his gloss meaningful.
